Am I required to carry it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Buy it now: most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there's no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 18,556 NFIP flood claims and $1.2 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2024, 2023 and 1985.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2024 ($1,075,668,701), 2023 ($20,941,859), 1985 ($12,773,689). Total paid $1,179,098,944: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 18,556 claims since 1978 against 65,247 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

52.0% of bills here can keep rising: they pay less than FEMA's full-risk price. Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. Median premium $886, full-risk $1,491 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$886
  • Median full-risk premium$1,491
  • Pay below full-risk52.0% of 42,387Florida: 49.8%

Years to the full-risk price: By law most premiums cannot rise more than 18% a year (FloodSmart puts it at 18–25% for most policyholders); the cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. At the 18% cap, a policy at today's median premium ($886) would take at least about 4 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk premium ($1,491). This is the limit on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for rivers and heavy rain and Relatively High for coastal flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskRelatively High
  • Inland flood riskRelatively High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. A place with many valuable buildings can have a large total loss and a low loss per dollar, so the rating and the percentile below can differ. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $7.8 million of flood loss a year across all its buildings; per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 66% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $146.3 million of flood loss a year across all its buildings; per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 27% of U.S. counties. Any loss figure is a whole-county estimate across all buildings, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How often do the same homes flood here?

Some homes here flood again and again: 4,337 flood-damage applications in FEMA's disaster-aid records came from homes that flooded more than once; 111 of those records came from homes hit in four or more.

  • Repeat-flood damage records4,337
  • Records from homes hit four or more times111

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid applications since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Repetitive-Loss Flood Properties. Data effective FEMA's current list; retrieved October 26, 2026.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our record counts match the API's own totals; FEMA's official policy count is not yet joined for Hillsborough County.

In-force count: 65,247 policy units (from 55,944 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 55,944 of 55,944 fetched; claims: 18,556 of 18,556 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
